newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania police move to secure airport.
newsitem.headline: Albania police move to secure airport.

text.p: Armed Albanian police moved to secure Tirana airport on Wednesday in order to reopen the country's main gateway to the outside world and to Western aid in hopes of restoring stability after a month of violence.

Armoured vehicles and truckloads of police, each with a Kalashnikov assault rifle, were dispatched to Rinas airport, 25 km (15 miles) west of the capital, the day before the government has pledged to reopen it to commercial airliners.

Three Italian Chinook military helicopters landed briefly at the airport, closed last Thursday amid mounting violence. Italian paratrooper guards handed over to Albanian police about 100 presumed criminals they said had taken advantage of the unrest to flee across the Adriatic.
Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, who heads an all-party government overseeing elections in June, remained in Tirana, apparenty cancelling plans to travel to southern Albania.

Rebels in the south have threatened to form their own alternative government unless President Sali Berisha resigns by Thursday. Officials in the rebel stronghold of Gjirokaster, Fino's home town, said they had been told the prime minister was too busy to make the trip.
Also in Tirana, a European Union delegation was winding up a three-day mission to determine how best to help consolidate order ahead of new elections in June and to feed Albania's 3.4 million people.

"The most important thing in this emergency is the presence of international mediators, monitors and observers who can help us work together in a political framework," Fatos Nano, Berisha's main political rival, told Reuters.
"The only solution to the crisis is through political means. We have to disarm the minds of Albanian institutions and the minds of politicians. Then people will hand in their guns."
Well over 100 people have died in violence sparked in the south by the collapse of fraudulent investment schemes which soaked up life savings of hundreds of thousands of Albanians.

Violence spread to the north last week and threatened to engulf Tirana before authorities restored order. Officials said pockets of violence persisted on Thursday, with 14 people killed by stray bullets in various towns.
Gjirokaster rebel leader Agim Gozhita, a former army general, told Reuters on Tuesday that if Berisha did not go they would elect a presidential council to challenge him.

Ghozita said he was willing to work with the new government only if it stopped all cooperation with Berisha, accused by the rebels of failing to stop the shady schemes or warn the public of the risks.
But he stressed that the rebels wanted a political and not a military solution to the crisis.
Berisha has pledged to step down if his Democratic Party, which has ruled for five years, loses the elections, but this has failed to satisfy the rebels.
In Italy, the government proclaimed a national state of emergency to deal with up to 10,000 Albanian refugees who have poured across the Adriatic, some in barely seaworthy boats.

The measure, which will allow the government to resort to emergency funding, was contained in a cabinet decree which also empowered authorities to repatriate any Albanians deemed to be a threat to public order.
The decree confirmed that Italy would grant temporary refuge to Albanians who have fled the anarchy.
Italy's chief anti-Mafia prosecutor, Pier Luigi Vigna, said he feared the exodus might include criminals released by the government during the lawlessness.
